lines.text: Between capital and the asset sits a crowd.
Brokers, valuers, lawyers, notaries, lenders. Some twenty parties stand between the money and the building.
Two businesses work this stretch. Prop.com sells outcome services: desk work, delivered faster and cheaper.
Propchain builds the rails: a standard everyone runs on, even Prop.com's competitors.
So for each party in the middle: own it, tool it, or onboard it? And in which order?
It starts with a rule. Every party in the middle splits in three.
The act carries the liability: a signature, a deed, an audit opinion. Its value is its independence. It stays independent, and we tool it.
The process prepares the act: data rooms, models, draft deeds. It's desk work: most of the hours, and the fee. It becomes a Prop.com service.
And the data: rent rolls in, N-O-I out. Comparables in, a mark out. Propchain attests it.
Take the valuer. The signature is independent. The model is not. And the mark is data.
An opinion issued by the party that profits from the deal is worth less, whatever its quality. Independence is the product.
Now lay the parties out in the order a deal moves: eight layers, from capital to the asset.
And every party gets one verb.
Investors, lenders, buyers, sellers, tenants: they aren't intermediaries. They are the market. Propchain onboards them.
The notary, registry, valuer, auditor, depositary and lawyers each hold an act that must stay theirs. We tool them. We never own them.
Everything else is process: underwriting, reporting, asset management, debt advisory, payments. Prop.com serves it as an outcome, automated underneath.
Prop.com sells the outcome of a desk, not the AI: four or five analyst seats, replaced by one outsourced desk.
Five criteria score each service line, and sort them into three tiers.
Tier one, now: underwriting, reporting, asset management and debt advisory. Pure desk work, no licence in the way.
Tier two, next: fund admin, D-D assembly, legal process and payments. A regulated act is in the way, so we deliver the process under a named partner's act.
Tier three, later: property management and origination. We want the records, not the headcount.
Land and expand: tier two sells to the same client, whose data we already hold.
Propchain's order follows a different logic: what each party unlocks.
Lenders first. Credit boxes rest on the platform, and every asset with attested N-O-I carries a debt quote.
Then valuers: marks on attested inputs, so loan-to-value tests run on marks lenders already trust.
Then notaries: financed, marked pairs settle without re-verification.
Then auditors and depositaries, reading the same records. Other managers join because their lenders did.
Last, property managers feed in source data, lawyers land due diligence as fields, and the registry connects.
Dependency, not rank. A notary tool with nothing to settle is a demo. With a financed bid and a mark, it's a closing.
For acts we can't own, the tools are free or near-free. The tool never produces the act. It prepares, presents and records it.
So the two businesses pull each other. Services make records. Records make rails worth joining. And parties on the rails need their process half delivered.
It works only if Prop.com is just a participant: same identity, same permissions, no privileged read. Every read is logged.
Own the desk. Tool the act. Onboard the market.
